countability: countable, and uncountable as a substance
gloss: A hard, shiny material such as iron, gold, or copper that conducts heat and electricity.
examples: The handle is *metal*, so it gets hot fast.
Copper and zinc are both *metals*.
You can hear the *metal* creaking when a truck crosses the bridge.
contrast: In American English the t is flapped, so *metal* sounds exactly like *medal* — only context separates them.

gloss: A strong alloy of iron and carbon used for tools, cars, and building frames.
examples: The frame is *steel*, so it won't warp.
Half the town used to work at the *steel* mill.
Stainless *steel* doesn't rust the way plain iron does.
contrast: *Steel* is a perfect homophone of *steal*.

gloss: A light, silvery metal used for cans, foil, and airplane parts.
examples: Put the *aluminum* cans in the blue bin.
The ladder is *aluminum*, so it's easy to carry.
*Aluminum* siding was on every house in that neighborhood.
contrast: Americans write *aluminum* (uh-LOO-mih-nuhm); the British write *aluminium* (al-yoo-MIN-ee-uhm), with an extra syllable.

gloss: A reddish-brown metal used mainly for wiring and water pipes.
examples: The plumber replaced the old pipes with *copper*.
*Copper* turns green after years outdoors.
Scrap *copper* is worth real money right now.

gloss: A yellow metal made from copper and zinc.
examples: The door handles are solid *brass*.
She polishes the *brass* on the boat every spring.
A *brass* band played in the park all afternoon.

gloss: A brown metal made from copper and tin, used for statues and medals.
examples: The statue in the square is *bronze*.
He took home the *bronze* in the 400 meters.
*Bronze* darkens as it ages.

gloss: A soft, yellow precious metal used for jewelry and coins.
examples: The ring is fourteen-karat *gold*.
*Gold* went up again this week.
They struck *gold* in these hills in 1849.

gloss: A shiny white precious metal used for jewelry, coins, and tableware.
examples: Grandma's *silver* only comes out at Thanksgiving.
The bracelet is sterling *silver*.
*Silver* tarnishes if you leave it out in the air.

gloss: A soft, silvery metal, often used as a coating on other metals.
examples: The roof is *tin*, so the rain is deafening.
Solder is mostly *tin* and lead.
The old toy soldiers were cast from *tin*.
contrast: In American English *tin* is the metal; the British also use *a tin* for what Americans call *a can*.

gloss: A heavy, soft, gray metal that is poisonous to people.
examples: Older houses may still have *lead* paint.
The water tested positive for *lead*.
*Lead* is surprisingly heavy for its size.
contrast: The metal *lead* is said LED, like the past tense *led* — not LEED, which is the verb *to lead*.

gloss: A bluish-white metal used to coat steel and in some medicines.
examples: Galvanized nails are coated in *zinc*.
She takes *zinc* whenever she feels a cold coming on.
The *zinc* keeps the steel from rusting.

countability: both — countable and uncountable with different meanings
gloss: A hard silvery metal, and also the American five-cent coin.
examples: The faucet is plated in *nickel*.
I found two *nickels* under the car seat.
Some people get a rash from the *nickel* in cheap earrings.
contrast: Uncountable as the metal (*plated in nickel*), countable as the coin (*two nickels*).

gloss: A very valuable silvery-white metal that does not corrode.
examples: The wedding band is *platinum*.
*Platinum* costs more than gold most years.
Catalytic converters contain a little *platinum*.

gloss: A strong, light metal used in aircraft, tools, and medical implants.
examples: His new hip is *titanium*.
The frame is *titanium*, which is why the bike is so light.
*Titanium* is hard on drill bits.

gloss: A silvery metal that is liquid at room temperature and highly toxic.
examples: Old thermometers were filled with *mercury*.
Some fish carry high levels of *mercury*.
Never touch spilled *mercury* with your hands.

gloss: A shiny metal coating put on metal parts for looks and protection.
examples: The bumper is all *chrome*.
He spent Sunday polishing the *chrome* on his bike.
The *chrome* has started to peel around the mirror.

gloss: The reddish-brown flaky coating that forms on iron when it gets wet.
examples: There's *rust* along the bottom of the door.
A little *rust* on the tools won't hurt anything.
Salt on the roads eats cars alive with *rust*.

gloss: Very thin sheet metal, usually aluminum, used for wrapping food.
examples: Cover the pan with *foil* and bake it another hour.
We're out of *foil* again.
Wrap the leftovers in *foil* before you put them in the fridge.

countability: countable, and uncountable as a substance
gloss: Metal drawn out into a thin, flexible strand.
examples: A squirrel chewed through the *wire*.
Tie the sign up with a piece of *wire*.
The *wires* behind the TV are a mess.

countability: countable, and uncountable as a substance
gloss: A large hardwood tree, or the strong wood that comes from it.
examples: The table is solid *oak*.
There's a hundred-year-old *oak* in the front yard.
*Oak* floors hold up better than pine.

countability: countable, and uncountable as a substance
gloss: An evergreen tree with needles, or the soft pale wood it produces.
examples: The shelves are cheap *pine*.
The whole cabin smells like *pine*.
They planted *pines* along the fence line.

countability: countable, and uncountable as a substance
gloss: A shade tree known for its syrup and its hard, pale wood.
examples: The cutting board is *maple*.
The *maples* turn bright red in October.
*Maple* is harder than pine, so it doesn't dent as easily.

countability: countable, and uncountable as a substance
gloss: An evergreen tree with fragrant wood that resists rot.
examples: We built the deck out of *cedar*.
The closet is lined with *cedar* to keep the moths out.
A row of *cedars* blocks the wind off the lake.

gloss: Board made by gluing thin layers of wood together.
examples: They boarded up the windows with *plywood*.
A sheet of *plywood* costs twice what it used to.
Under the carpet it's just *plywood*.

gloss: Trees or heavy cut wood used for building.
examples: The company owns thousands of acres of *timber*.
Heavy *timber* holds up the whole roof.
*Timber* prices jumped last spring.
contrast: Americans say *lumber* for cut boards and keep *timber* for standing trees or heavy beams; British English uses *timber* for both.

gloss: Wood that has been sawn into boards for building.
examples: I need to pick up some *lumber* at the hardware store.
The *lumber* is stacked behind the garage.
*Lumber* got expensive during the pandemic.
contrast: *Lumber* is the everyday American word; British English says *timber*.

gloss: A tall, fast-growing grass with hard hollow stems used as a material.
examples: The floors are *bamboo*.
*Bamboo* grows so fast it takes over the yard.
The cutting board is made of *bamboo*.
contrast: Stress falls on the second syllable: bam-BOO.

countability: both — countable and uncountable with different meanings
gloss: The light, spongy bark of a certain oak, or a stopper made from it.
examples: The bulletin board is *cork*.
The *cork* broke off in the bottle.
Save the *corks* — she's making a wreath out of them.
contrast: Uncountable as the material (*a cork floor*), countable as a bottle stopper (*two corks*).

gloss: The tough outer covering of a tree trunk and its branches.
examples: The deer stripped the *bark* off the young trees.
*Bark* mulch keeps the weeds down.
You can tell a birch by its white *bark*.

gloss: A black form of carbon made by burning wood slowly, used as fuel.
examples: Light the *charcoal* half an hour before you cook.
We're out of *charcoal* for the grill.
She sketched the whole portrait in *charcoal*.

gloss: Dense wood from broad-leaved trees such as oak or maple.
examples: The apartment has *hardwood* floors.
*Hardwood* burns longer than pine.
Refinishing the *hardwood* took a week.

countability: countable, and uncountable as a substance
gloss: Cloth made by weaving or knitting fibers together.
examples: She picked a heavy *fabric* for the curtains.
This *fabric* wrinkles if you look at it.
The store sells *fabrics* by the yard.

countability: both — countable and uncountable with different meanings
gloss: Woven material, or a small piece of it used for cleaning.
examples: Wipe it down with a damp *cloth*.
The bag is made of heavy *cloth*.
Keep a few clean *cloths* under the sink.
contrast: *Cloths* (KLAWTHS) means rags or pieces of fabric; *clothes* (KLOHZ) means the things you wear.

gloss: A soft white fiber from a plant, and the cloth woven from it.
examples: The shirt is a hundred percent *cotton*.
*Cotton* breathes better than polyester in the summer.
They grow *cotton* all across the Delta.

gloss: The soft hair of sheep, and the yarn or cloth made from it.
examples: The sweater is *wool*, so wash it cold.
*Wool* itches the back of my neck.
A *wool* coat will get you through a Chicago winter.
contrast: The vowel is short, like *full* — not long like *pool*.

gloss: A fine, smooth cloth made from the thread of silkworms.
examples: The scarf is real *silk*.
*Silk* stains if you get water on it.
She wore a *silk* blouse to the interview.

gloss: Cloth woven from flax, and by extension sheets and tablecloths.
examples: He showed up in a rumpled *linen* suit.
*Linen* wrinkles the second you sit down.
The clean *linen* is in the hall closet.

gloss: Animal skin treated so it can be used for shoes, bags, and jackets.
examples: The seats are real *leather*.
*Leather* softens once you break it in.
She carries a black *leather* bag.

gloss: The heavy blue cotton cloth that jeans are made of.
examples: The jacket is stiff new *denim*.
*Denim* fades where you sit.
He wore *denim* head to toe.

gloss: A strong artificial fiber used in rope, brushes, and clothing.
examples: The tent is lightweight *nylon*.
*Nylon* dries fast, which is why hikers like it.
The strap is *nylon* webbing.

gloss: A synthetic fiber used in clothing that resists wrinkles.
examples: The shirt is a cotton and *polyester* blend.
*Polyester* doesn't breathe in the heat.
Everything in that decade was *polyester*.
contrast: Main stress lands on the third syllable: pah-lee-ES-tur.

gloss: A thick fabric with a soft, raised surface on one side.
examples: The curtains are deep red *velvet*.
*Velvet* shows every fingerprint.
She had on a black *velvet* dress.

countability: countable, and uncountable as a substance
gloss: The thick hair covering an animal, or a garment made from it.
examples: The cat leaves *fur* on everything.
Her grandmother's *furs* are still up in the attic.
The collar is trimmed with *fur*.

gloss: A delicate openwork fabric with patterns of holes in it.
examples: The dress has *lace* at the collar.
The tablecloth is old *lace*.
*Lace* snags on everything.

countability: both — countable and uncountable with different meanings
gloss: Strong, coarse cloth used for tents and bags, or a piece of it stretched for painting.
examples: The bag is heavy *canvas*.
There were half-finished *canvases* all over the studio.
The awning is faded *canvas*.
contrast: One s: *canvas* is the cloth. *Canvass*, with two, is the verb for going door to door.

gloss: A thick cloth made by pressing wool fibers together instead of weaving them.
examples: The pool table is covered in green *felt*.
Cut the shapes out of *felt*.
There's a piece of *felt* under each chair leg.
contrast: Written and said exactly like *felt*, the past tense of *feel* — only the sentence tells you which one it is.

gloss: Leather with a soft, brushed surface.
examples: The boots are *suede*, so keep them out of the rain.
*Suede* stains permanently.
He wore a brown *suede* jacket.
contrast: Five letters, one syllable: SWAYD. The ue is silent.

countability: countable, and uncountable as a substance
gloss: A thin strand of cotton or other fiber used for sewing.
examples: Do you have any black *thread*?
A loose *thread* is hanging off the hem.
Pull the *threads* out and start the seam over.
contrast: The ea says EH here, so *thread* rhymes with *bed*, not with *bead*.

countability: countable, and uncountable as a substance
gloss: Thick spun fiber used for knitting.
examples: She bought *yarn* for a baby blanket.
The cat got into the *yarn* again.
That shop carries hand-dyed *yarns*.

gloss: A soft, warm synthetic fabric, or the woolly coat of a sheep.
examples: The jacket is lined with *fleece*.
*Fleece* dries faster than wool.
He pulled on a *fleece* pullover and went out.

gloss: A soft, brushed cotton cloth used for shirts and sheets.
examples: He lives in *flannel* shirts all winter.
We put the *flannel* sheets on in November.
*Flannel* gets softer every time you wash it.

gloss: A very fine, soft wool from a kind of goat.
examples: The sweater is *cashmere*, so hand-wash it.
*Cashmere* is warm without being bulky.
A good *cashmere* scarf lasts for years.

countability: countable, and uncountable as a substance
gloss: A light artificial material that can be molded into almost any shape.
examples: The whole toy is cheap *plastic*.
Paper or *plastic*?
Some *plastics* can't be recycled at all.

gloss: A stretchy, waterproof material made from tree sap or produced synthetically.
examples: The soles are thick *rubber*.
*Rubber* cracks when it gets old.
Put a *rubber* mat down in the tub.
contrast: In American English *rubber* is the material; in British English *a rubber* is also a pencil eraser.

gloss: A tough plastic used for flooring, siding, and records.
examples: The kitchen floor is *vinyl*.
He still buys his music on *vinyl*.
*Vinyl* siding never needs painting.
contrast: Said VY-nuhl, with the first syllable like *vine* — not VIN-il.

gloss: A light material full of tiny bubbles, either soft padding or a froth on liquid.
examples: The mattress is memory *foam*.
Spray *foam* seals the gaps around the pipes.
There was two inches of *foam* on top of the beer.

gloss: A rubbery synthetic material used for seals, molds, and bakeware.
examples: Run a bead of *silicone* around the tub.
The spatula is *silicone*, so it won't melt.
*Silicone* caulk takes a day to cure.
contrast: *Silicone* (SIL-ih-kohn) is the rubbery material; *silicon* (SIL-ih-kun) is the element in computer chips.

gloss: A milky liquid from rubber trees, and the paint or rubber made from it.
examples: We used *latex* paint on the walls.
Some people are allergic to *latex* gloves.
*Latex* cleans up with plain water.
contrast: The first syllable is like *late*: LAY-teks.

gloss: A material of fine glass threads, used for insulation and boat hulls.
examples: The attic is insulated with *fiberglass*.
The hull is *fiberglass*, not wood.
Wear gloves — *fiberglass* itches for days.
contrast: American spelling *fiberglass*; British *fibreglass*.

countability: countable, and uncountable as a substance
gloss: A clear plastic, or the fast-drying paint made from it.
examples: The tub surround is *acrylic*.
She paints in *acrylics* now instead of oils.
The sweater is *acrylic*, not wool.

countability: countable, and uncountable as a substance
gloss: Hard mineral material from the ground, or a piece of it.
examples: The old church is built of *stone*.
He skipped *stones* across the pond.
There's a *stone* wall along the property line.

countability: countable, and uncountable as a substance
gloss: The hard material that makes up the earth's surface, or a loose piece of it.
examples: They hit solid *rock* two feet down.
Somebody threw a *rock* through the window.
The kids climbed all over the *rocks*.

countability: both — countable and uncountable with different meanings
gloss: A hard stone that polishes to a smooth shine, or a small glass ball.
examples: The countertops are *marble*.
He found a jar of his father's old *marbles*.
The lobby floor is white *marble*.
contrast: Uncountable as the stone (*a marble floor*), countable as the little glass ball (*a bag of marbles*).

gloss: A very hard speckled rock used for counters and monuments.
examples: They put in *granite* counters.
The steps are worn *granite*.
*Granite* is nearly impossible to scratch.

gloss: Sticky earth that hardens when it is dried or fired.
examples: The soil out here is heavy *clay*.
She threw a bowl out of *clay*.
*Clay* holds water instead of draining.

gloss: A hard, glassy mineral found in many rocks and used in watches.
examples: There's a vein of white *quartz* running through the rock.
The watch is *quartz*, not mechanical.
*Quartz* countertops are engineered, not quarried.
contrast: One syllable, KWORTS — the qu says KW.

gloss: A gray rock that splits into flat sheets, used for roofs and floors.
examples: The roof is original *slate*.
The patio is laid with *slate*.
*Slate* cracks if you drop something heavy on it.

gloss: Small loose stones used for roads and driveways.
examples: The driveway is just *gravel*.
You can hear the *gravel* crunch when a car pulls in.
They spread fresh *gravel* on the road last week.

countability: countable, and uncountable as a substance
gloss: A solid with a regular geometric shape, or fine cut glass.
examples: Sugar forms big *crystals* if you cook it too long.
The glasses are lead *crystal*.
Frost made *crystals* all over the window.

gloss: The hardest known mineral, a clear precious stone used in jewelry.
examples: The ring has a small *diamond*.
*Diamonds* will cut through almost anything.
She lost a *diamond* out of her earring.
contrast: Most Americans say it in two syllables, DY-muhnd, though the fuller DY-uh-muhnd is equally correct.

gloss: A black rock burned as fuel.
examples: The plant still burns *coal*.
His grandfather mined *coal* in West Virginia.
*Coal* dust got into everything.

gloss: A soft white rock, or the sticks of it used for writing.
examples: There's no *chalk* left at the board.
The kids drew all over the driveway with *chalk*.
Climbers put *chalk* on their hands for grip.
contrast: The l is silent: CHAWK, rhyming with *talk*.

gloss: A precious stone that has been cut and polished.
examples: The crown is set with *gems*.
He collects rough *gems* and cuts them himself.
That green *gem* is an emerald.

gloss: A small, round, white gem that forms inside an oyster.
examples: She wore her mother's *pearls*.
A single *pearl* hung on a thin chain.
Real *pearls* feel slightly gritty against your teeth.

gloss: A natural solid substance found in the ground, such as quartz or salt.
examples: The rock is full of shiny *minerals*.
Spinach is a good source of iron and other *minerals*.
The well water has a strong *mineral* taste.

gloss: A yellow chemical element that smells of rotten eggs when it burns.
examples: The hot springs reek of *sulfur*.
*Sulfur* is used to make matches.
There's *sulfur* in the well water.
contrast: Americans spell it *sulfur*; the British write *sulphur*. Both are said SUL-fur.

gloss: A fibrous mineral once used for insulation, now known to cause cancer.
examples: The old pipes are wrapped in *asbestos*.
They had to test the building for *asbestos*.
*Asbestos* removal costs a fortune.
contrast: Stress on the second syllable: as-BES-tuhs.

gloss: The hard, creamy-white substance of elephant tusks.
examples: The handle is carved *ivory*.
Selling *ivory* is illegal almost everywhere now.
The walls are painted a soft *ivory*.

gloss: Wet, soft earth.
examples: The truck is covered in *mud*.
Take your boots off — there's *mud* all over them.
The field turns to *mud* every spring.

gloss: The top layer of earth in which plants grow.
examples: The *soil* here is too sandy for tomatoes.
Add compost to improve the *soil*.
Erosion has washed away the best *soil*.

gloss: Loose earth, or any substance that makes something unclean.
examples: The kids came in with *dirt* under their nails.
It's a *dirt* road for the last two miles.
Sweep the *dirt* into the dustpan.

countability: countable, and uncountable as a substance
gloss: A chemical that tastes sour and can burn or dissolve other substances.
examples: Battery *acid* ate a hole in the floor mat.
Lemon juice is a mild *acid*.
Some *acids* will burn right through metal.

gloss: A substance produced by or used in chemistry.
examples: The pool needs *chemicals* every week.
A truck spilled some kind of *chemical* on the highway.
Read the label before you mix *chemicals*.
contrast: The ch says K: KEM-ih-kuhl.

gloss: A strong chemical liquid used to whiten cloth and kill germs.
examples: A little *bleach* will get that stain out.
Never mix *bleach* with ammonia.
The whole kitchen smelled like *bleach*.

gloss: A colorless gas with a sharp smell, used dissolved in water as a cleaner.
examples: The cage smelled of *ammonia*.
She cleans the windows with *ammonia*.
*Ammonia* fumes will make your eyes water.
contrast: Stress on the second syllable: uh-MOH-nee-uh.

gloss: The intoxicating substance in drinks, or a clear liquid used to disinfect.
examples: Wipe the thermometer with rubbing *alcohol*.
The punch has no *alcohol* in it.
*Alcohol* evaporates fast.

gloss: The lightest chemical element, a colorless gas.
examples: Water is *hydrogen* and oxygen.
The city bought a few buses that run on *hydrogen*.
*Hydrogen* burns with almost no visible flame.

gloss: The gas in the air that living things need in order to breathe.
examples: She's on *oxygen* at night.
There's less *oxygen* at that altitude.
A fire needs fuel and *oxygen*.

gloss: A chemical element found in coal, diamonds, and every living thing.
examples: Diamonds are pure *carbon*.
The bike frame is *carbon* fiber.
They're trying to cut *carbon* emissions in half.

gloss: The colorless gas that makes up most of the air.
examples: *Nitrogen* is about eighty percent of the atmosphere.
The fertilizer is high in *nitrogen*.
The shop fills the tires with *nitrogen*.

gloss: The liquid fuel that most cars run on.
examples: *Gasoline* is up another twenty cents.
The mower ran out of *gasoline*.
Don't store *gasoline* in the house.
contrast: Americans say *gasoline*, usually shortened to *gas*; the British say *petrol*.

countability: countable, and uncountable as a substance
gloss: Any material burned to produce heat or power.
examples: The plane took on *fuel* in Denver.
Coal and oil are fossil *fuels*.
*Fuel* costs eat up most of the budget.

gloss: A soft solid that melts easily, used in candles and polish.
examples: There's *wax* all over the tablecloth.
He put a coat of *wax* on the car.
Ear *wax* had built up and muffled her hearing.

countability: countable, and uncountable as a substance
gloss: A sticky substance used to join things together.
examples: Let the *glue* dry overnight.
I've got *glue* all over my fingers.
Wood *glues* end up stronger than the wood itself.

countability: countable, and uncountable as a substance
gloss: A substance used to change the color of cloth or hair.
examples: The *dye* ran and turned the whole load pink.
She uses a *dye* to cover the gray.
Some food *dyes* are banned in Europe.
contrast: *Dye* sounds exactly like *die*; only the spelling separates them.

countability: countable, and uncountable as a substance
gloss: A chemical cleaner used for laundry or dishes.
examples: We're out of laundry *detergent*.
Use less *detergent* than the box says.
Some *detergents* irritate sensitive skin.

countability: countable, and uncountable as a substance
gloss: A substance that causes illness or death if it gets into the body.
examples: Keep the rat *poison* away from the dog.
Those berries are *poison*.
Most household *poisons* are stored under the sink.

gloss: A heavy fuel oil burned in truck and bus engines.
examples: The truck takes *diesel*, not gas.
*Diesel* costs more than regular right now.
You can smell the *diesel* from the parking lot.
contrast: The s is said as a Z: DEE-zuhl.

gloss: A hard building material made from cement, sand, gravel, and water.
examples: They poured the *concrete* for the driveway this morning.
The floor is bare *concrete*.
*Concrete* takes about a month to reach full strength.
contrast: As a noun the stress is up front: KAHN-kreet.

gloss: The gray powder that binds sand and gravel into concrete.
examples: Pick up two more bags of *cement*.
Mix the *cement* with water until it's like batter.
A thin layer of *cement* holds the bricks together.
contrast: Stress on the second syllable: sih-MENT, not SEE-ment.

countability: countable, and uncountable as a substance
gloss: A hard block of baked clay used for building, or that material in general.
examples: The house is red *brick*.
A few *bricks* came loose in the chimney.
They laid the *brick* by hand.

gloss: The paste of cement and sand that holds bricks or stones together.
examples: The *mortar* between the bricks is crumbling.
He scraped out the old *mortar* and repacked it.
Fresh *mortar* has to stay damp while it cures.

gloss: A paste spread on walls and ceilings that hardens as it dries.
examples: The *plaster* is cracking above the door.
These old walls are *plaster*, not drywall.
He patched the hole with *plaster*.

gloss: Panels of gypsum board used to make interior walls.
examples: They hung the *drywall* in a single day.
There's a hole in the *drywall* behind the door.
Cutting *drywall* makes a huge mess.
contrast: *Drywall* is the American word; the British say *plasterboard*.

gloss: The black sticky material mixed with gravel to surface roads.
examples: The *asphalt* softens in the heat.
They repaved the lot with fresh *asphalt*.
You can smell the *asphalt* from a block away.

gloss: A thick, black, sticky substance made from coal or oil.
examples: There's *tar* stuck to the bottom of my shoe.
They spread hot *tar* across the roof.
Cigarette smoke leaves *tar* in your lungs.

gloss: Material put in walls or around pipes to stop heat or sound from passing through.
examples: The attic needs more *insulation*.
The old *insulation* had settled to the bottom of the wall.
Good *insulation* cuts the heating bill in half.
contrast: Uncountable in English: say *some insulation* or *a roll of insulation*, never *an insulation*.

countability: countable, and uncountable as a substance
gloss: Colored liquid spread on a surface to color or protect it.
examples: The *paint* is still tacky.
We need another gallon of *paint*.
Acrylic *paints* dry much faster than oils.

countability: countable, and uncountable as a substance
gloss: A flat piece of baked clay or stone used to cover floors, walls, or roofs.
examples: A couple of *tiles* cracked near the tub.
The whole bathroom is *tile*.
They laid the *tile* diagonally.

countability: countable, and uncountable as a substance
gloss: A substance in the form of very fine dry particles.
examples: Grind the pills into a fine *powder*.
Stir the *powder* into a cup of warm water.
There was a white *powder* all over the counter.

countability: countable, and uncountable as a substance
gloss: A substance that flows freely, such as water or oil.
examples: Don't set any *liquid* down near the laptop.
You can't take *liquids* through security.
The medicine comes as a pill or a *liquid*.

gloss: A particular kind of material with definite properties.
examples: There was a sticky *substance* on the door handle.
Bleach and ammonia are both dangerous *substances*.
The lab identified the *substance* as ordinary sugar.

countability: countable, and uncountable as a substance
gloss: Any substance from which something is made.
examples: What *material* is the roof made of?
They ran out of building *materials* halfway through.
The jacket is made of a waterproof *material*.

gloss: A substance made of two or more elements chemically combined.
examples: Water is a *compound* of hydrogen and oxygen.
The soil test turned up several *compounds* nobody expected.
Salt is a simple *compound*.
contrast: The noun is stressed on the first syllable, KAHM-pownd; the verb *to compound* is stressed on the second, kuhm-POWND.

gloss: A pure substance that cannot be broken down into anything simpler.
examples: Gold is an *element*; brass is not.
About ninety *elements* occur in nature.
Carbon is the *element* all life is built on.

gloss: Frozen water.
examples: Could I get a little more *ice*?
There's black *ice* on the bridge.
The *ice* on the pond isn't thick enough yet.

gloss: The hot gas water turns into when it boils.
examples: *Steam* was pouring out from under the hood.
The bathroom filled with *steam*.
The building is heated by *steam*.

countability: countable, and uncountable as a substance
gloss: A substance in gas form that is normally a liquid or a solid.
examples: Water *vapor* condenses on the cold glass.
The paint *vapors* gave everybody a headache.
You could see the *vapor* rising off the lake.
contrast: Americans write *vapor*; the British write *vapour*.

countability: countable, and uncountable as a substance
gloss: A thin thread of natural or artificial material, or the part of food that aids digestion.
examples: Carpet *fibers* turned up on the suspect's jacket.
Beans are high in *fiber*.
The rope is made of natural *fiber*.
contrast: American *fiber*, British *fibre* — same pronunciation.

gloss: Thick oily matter, especially melted animal fat or machine lubricant.
examples: There's *grease* splattered all over the stove.
Pack the wheel bearings with *grease*.
The bottom of the pan was thick with *grease*.
contrast: The noun *grease* ends in an S sound; many Americans say the verb *to grease* with a Z.

gloss: Stiff, thick paper used for boxes and packing.
examples: Break the *cardboard* down before you recycle it.
The whole thing showed up in a *cardboard* box.
Wet *cardboard* falls apart in your hands.

countability: countable, and uncountable as a substance
gloss: A soft absorbent material full of holes, or a piece of it used for cleaning.
examples: Wipe the counter with a damp *sponge*.
The *sponge* by the sink smells terrible.
Grab a pack of *sponges* while you're out.

gloss: A hard, white ceramic used for fine dishes and bathroom fixtures.
examples: The sink is old *porcelain*.
She collects *porcelain* figurines.
*Porcelain* chips if you drop something heavy in the sink.
contrast: Usually three syllables in American speech, POR-suh-lin, with the middle one very light.

countability: countable, and uncountable as a substance
gloss: Hard material made by firing clay, or objects made from it.
examples: The mug is *ceramic*, not plastic.
She sells her *ceramics* at the farmers market.
*Ceramic* tile stays cold underfoot.
contrast: Stress on the second syllable: suh-RAM-ik.
